questions.topic: The chance a species is missed across repeat visits
questions.learningObjective: design a repeat-visit argument using a per-visit detection probability
questions.stem: Memo: repeat garden visits detect a target bird species on 40 per cent of visits. Describe how the planner should use that detection rate to argue for the number of visits needed in the scheme's monitoring protocol.

answer.exemplar: The chance of missing the species on one visit is 0.60, so over k visits the chance of missing it every time is 0.60 to the power k. Setting that below a chosen threshold, for example 0.05, gives about six visits, and the planner should present the probability of at least one detection alongside the count so the committee sees how quickly confidence builds.

questions.explanation: Repeated visits give independent chances to detect, so the chance of missing the species on all of them is the miss probability raised to the number of visits. That decay justifies repeat visits.
questions.hint: Raise the miss probability to the power of the visit count.

questions.stem: Memo: a wildlife survey recorded 18 species in the first hour, 24 after two hours and 27 after four hours. Explain why the raw richness figures cannot be compared across sites surveyed for different lengths of time and what should be reported instead.

answer.exemplar: The gains show a strong diminishing return: 6 extra species in the second hour but only 3 across the next two hours, so effort and richness are confounded and raw totals are not comparable. questions.topic: A rarefied richness from a pooled sample
questions.learningObjective: design a rarefaction comparison across parks surveyed for different times
questions.stem: Memo: three parks were surveyed for different lengths of time, so their raw species totals cannot be compared. Describe a design that produces a comparable richness figure for each park.

answer.exemplar: Pool the individuals from each park, note how many individuals belong to each species, and rarefy every park down to the smallest pooled sample size, using the expected number of species in a random draw of that many individuals. Repeat the rarefaction across many draws or use the analytic curve, and report the rarefied richness with its confidence interval alongside the raw total.

questions.explanation: Rarefaction answers how many species a fixed number of individuals would contain, so it removes the effort difference. Analytic or repeated subsampling gives the expectation and its spread, which the planner can publish.
questions.hint: Subsample every park down to the same number of individuals.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A Bray-Curtis dissimilarity from an abundance matrix
questions.learningObjective: explain how the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity is constructed and bounded
questions.stem: Memo: two embankment plantings hold counts of 40, 20, 15, 5 and 5 and of 10, 25, 20, 10 and 5 respectively. Explain how the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity is built and what the resulting value tells the committee.

answer.exemplar: Bray-Curtis sums the absolute differences between the two abundance vectors, which here gives 30 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 0 = 45, and divides by the sum of all individuals in both plantings, which is 155, so the value is 0.29. A low figure means the two plantings hold similar species in similar numbers, and the measure ranges from zero for identical plantings to one for completely disjoint ones.

questions.explanation: The numerator is the sum of absolute differences between paired counts and the denominator the combined abundance, giving 45/155 = 0.29. The measure runs from zero for identical plantings to one for disjoint ones.
questions.hint: Sum the paired differences and divide by the combined abundance.

questions.stem: Memo: the committee wants a single measure of how dominated each of twenty neighbourhood plantings is. Describe a design and reporting plan that compares dominance without being distorted by plot size.

answer.exemplar: For each planting compute the share of the commonest species and Simpson's D from the relative abundances, so plot size cancels out, and report both on one table with the raw counts alongside. answer.exemplar: The cumulative curve adds each species in turn, so it climbs to 62 per cent after only two species and passes three quarters with the fourth. questions.topic: A richness comparison made at unequal search effort
questions.learningObjective: explain how to make a survey comparison fair across unequal effort
questions.stem: Memo: residents argue that the wildlife corridor survey is unfair because some gardens were surveyed for longer than others. Explain how the survey could be made fair and what objection the planner should expect.

answer.exemplar: The fairest fix is to standardise effort, either by capping every garden at the same number of visits or by rarefying the pooled individuals down to the smallest sample, and then reporting the rarefied richness alongside the raw totals so nothing is hidden. The expected objection is that rarefaction discards real data, and the answer is that the raw totals are still published and that a differing effort must never masquerade as a difference in diversity.

questions.explanation: Unequal effort inflates the totals of better-searched gardens, so the comparison must be standardised by rarefaction or capped visits. Publishing raw and standardised figures defuses the objection that data was lost.
questions.hint: Standardise the effort, then publish both versions of the result.

questions.stem: Memo: the scheme must compare the planting diversity of verges that received different amounts of care. Describe a design that produces a fair diversity comparison.

answer.exemplar: Record every individual and its species in each verge, then subsample each verge's individuals down to the smallest common sample size and average the species found across many draws, giving a rarefied richness and its spread for each verge. questions.explanation: Rarefaction removes the effort difference while keeping every species record available. Averaging many draws gives a spread as well as a point estimate, and the raw totals keep the result auditable.
questions.hint: Subsample every verge to the same number of individuals.

answer.exemplar: Survey matched pairs of old and new planting plots at the same time of year and with the same survey effort, then compute both dominance measures for each plot from relative abundances so plot size does not interfere. questions.stem: Memo: the reserve's protocol must reach 95 per cent cumulative detection of a bird detected on 10 per cent of visits. Explain how the required number of visits is derived and why the result may be optimistic.

answer.exemplar: The miss probability of 0.90 must be raised to the number of visits until it falls below 0.05, which needs 29 visits because 0.90 to the 28th is 0.052 and the 29th is 0.047. The figure is optimistic because it assumes every visit is an independent chance at the same detection rate, so a single stormy day or a change in breeding behaviour breaks the assumption and the true number of visits needed will be larger.

questions.explanation: The miss probability raised to the number of visits must fall below the allowed failure level of 0.05, which needs 29 visits from 0.90. The calculation assumes independent visits at a constant detection rate.
questions.hint: Raise 0.90 to the power n until it drops below 0.05.

questions.stem: Memo: residents want proof that a rare plant really is absent from a meadow rather than simply overlooked. Describe a design and reporting plan that makes the absence claim defensible.

answer.exemplar: Survey the meadow the same number of times across a full flowering period, recording the date and weather of every visit and the detection history of the target plant. questions.explanation: The detection history turns an absence into a probability, and the per-visit detection rate makes the miss chance meaningful. Repeating visits across the flowering period controls seasonal timing.
questions.hint: Report a detection probability, not just a presence list.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The visits needed for a target cumulative detection
questions.learningObjective: calculate a required visit count from a per-visit detection rate
questions.stem: Memo: a species is detected on 45 per cent of visits and the protocol needs 90 per cent cumulative detection. Which number of visits does the calculation give?

options.text: Two visits, because 45 plus 45 per cent already exceeds 90 per cent.
options.misconception: adds detection rates instead of compounding misses

options.text: Four visits, because 0.55 to the fourth power falls below the 0.10 miss allowance.
Twelve visits, because the miss rate must be halved twice for every doubling of visits.
options.misconception: invents a halving rule for the miss probability

options.text: Twenty visits, because a detection rate under half always needs twenty visits.
options.misconception: applies a fixed visit count regardless of the rate

questions.explanation: The chance of missing the species every visit is 0.55 to the power n, which must fall below 0.10. The third visit leaves 0.166 and the fourth leaves 0.092, so four visits are needed.
questions.hint: Find the smallest n for which 0.55 to the n is under 0.10.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Detection-corrected occupancy against the naive count
questions.learningObjective: correct an occupancy proportion for a known detection rate
questions.stem: Memo: 80 allotment gardens were surveyed once and the species was found in 32 of them, with a per-visit detection probability of 0.80. How should the planner present the occupancy figure?

options.text: Occupancy is 0.32 and no correction is needed, because 32 gardens did hold the plant.
options.misconception: ignores imperfect detection entirely

options.text: Occupancy is 0.80, because the detection probability is the only reliable figure here.
options.misconception: mistakes detection probability for occupancy

options.text: Occupancy is 0.40, because the detection probability must be halved before applying it.
options.misconception: invents a halving step in the correction

options.text: Naive occupancy is 0.40 and the corrected estimate is 0.50, so half the true sites were missed.

questions.explanation: Thirty-two of 80 gives naive occupancy of 0.40, and dividing by the 0.80 detection probability gives 0.50. The correction raises the estimate because one visit can only miss occupied gardens.
questions.hint: Divide the naive proportion by the detection probability.

questions.topic: A Bray-Curtis dissimilarity from an abundance matrix
questions.learningObjective: compute Bray-Curtis for two orchards with equal totals
questions.stem: Memo: two community orchards hold counts of 45, 35, 20 and of 20, 35, 45, each with 100 trees. What is the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between the two orchards?
questions.explanation: The absolute differences are 25, 0 and 25, summing to 50, and the orchards hold 200 trees between them, so Bray-Curtis is 0.25. The middle species matches exactly.
questions.hint: Divide the summed differences by the combined total.

questions.topic: Two measures of dominance in the same sample
questions.learningObjective: compare paired dominance panels for the same four plots
questions.stem: A figure shows two panels. Panel A is a bar chart of the top-species share for four plots, reading 0.20, 0.35, 0.55 and 0.80. Panel B is a bar chart of Simpson's D for the same four plots, reading 0.25, 0.40, 0.55 and 0.70. Which reading is correct?

options.text: Both panels rank the plots the same way, and the fourth plot is the most dominated in each.
The two panels must disagree, because one measures the top species and the other the whole sample.
options.misconception: believes the two measures must rank samples differently

options.text: Panel B must be inverted, because Simpson's D falls as dominance rises.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of Simpson's D

options.text: The fourth plot must hold only one species, because a share of 0.80 leaves no room for others.
options.misconception: reads a high share as proof of a single species

questions.explanation: Both measures rise with dominance, so the plots rank identically in the two panels. A share of 0.80 leaves room for other species, so the fourth plot is dominant and not a monoculture.
questions.hint: Compare the ordering of the bars in both panels.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A richness comparison made at unequal search effort
questions.learningObjective: explain the reasoning for standardising two unequal-effort surveys
questions.stem: Memo: the conservation officer asks how the scheme can prove that two woodlands differ in diversity when one was surveyed for six hours and the other for one. Explain the reasoning the planner should present.

answer.exemplar: The two woodlands must be compared on a common footing, and the standard way to do that is to rarefy the six-hour sample down to the number of individuals or the effort of the one-hour sample and ask how many species that reduced sample would hold. Because species keep arriving as effort grows, the raw totals cannot be compared, but the rarefied figures remove the difference in searching and let the actual difference in diversity show.

questions.explanation: Raw totals confound effort with diversity, so the six-hour list will always look richer. Rarefying to a common effort removes that confound and lets the underlying difference appear.
questions.hint: Separate the effect of searching from the effect of diversity.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A rarefied richness from a pooled sample
questions.learningObjective: justify rarefaction to a committee that distrusts apparent data loss
questions.stem: Memo: the department must justify rarefaction to committee members who distrust the loss of data it appears to cause. Describe a design and reporting plan that makes the method defensible.

answer.exemplar: Explain that rarefaction does not delete records but answers a different question, namely how many species a fixed number of individuals would contain, and show the rarefaction curves for each site so the shape of the evidence is visible. Report the rarefied richness with its confidence interval next to the raw totals and the species found only in the larger samples, so nothing is concealed and the reader can judge the conclusion.

questions.explanation: Rarefaction reframes the comparison rather than discarding data, and publishing the curves makes the reasoning visible. Showing rarefied values beside raw totals keeps the claim checkable.
questions.hint: Show the curves and the raw totals side by side.
